# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy for Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a major global health burden, and despite advances in guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT), many patients remain symptomatic. Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) has been a mainstay of device therapy, but CRT is established for patients with QRS duration greater than 120 ms, yet most patients with heart failure have a QRS duration below 120 ms, and 30% or more of CRT recipients are nonresponders. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) was developed to address this therapeutic gap. CCM represents an innovative device-based therapy for patients with HF who remain symptomatic despite optimal GDMT, delivering biphasic, non-excitatory electrical signals during the absolute refractory period to enhance myocardial contractility and relaxation. [1]

## Mechanisms of action

Unlike pacing, CCM does not initiate a new contraction. CCM signals influence the biology of the failing myocardium and have been shown to induce an acute, mild augmentation of left ventricular (LV) contractile strength without an increase in myocardial oxygen consumption in both animal HF models and patients with reduced ejection fraction. [2,3] Acute effects appear to involve alterations of myocardial calcium handling, whereas over intermediate and longer time frames, CCM exerts a multitude of biochemical and molecular effects, including shifts of abnormally expressed genes toward normal. [3] In a human myocardial biopsy study, three months of CCM therapy induced reverse molecular remodeling, driving the genotype from the abnormal fetal program characteristic of heart failure toward a more normal adult profile, with the magnitude of gene expression change correlating with clinical effectiveness. [4] At the molecular level, CCM improves calcium cycling via enhanced SERCA2a activity and phospholamban phosphorylation, facilitating diastolic calcium reuptake. [1,5]

## Clinical evidence in HFrEF

The FIX-HF clinical trial program established the foundation for CCM. FIX-CHF-4, the first randomized controlled trial of CCM, was a double-blind, double-crossover study in which subjects were assigned to CCM on for 3 months then off, or the reversed sequence, with co-primary endpoints of change in peak VO2 and the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire. [6] One hundred and sixty-four subjects with ejection fraction below 35% and NYHA class II or III symptoms received a CCM pulse generator. [6]

The pivotal US trial, FIX-HF-5, then tested CCM on a broader scale. CCM was tested in 428 NYHA class III or IV, narrow-QRS HF patients with ejection fraction ≤35% randomized to optimal medical therapy plus CCM versus OMT alone; the primary safety endpoint was a test of noninferiority for the composite of all-cause mortality and hospitalizations. [7] Although the overall primary efficacy endpoint was not met, a detailed subgroup analysis revealed significantly greater treatment effects among patients with baseline EF ≥25%, constituting almost half of the entire cohort. [8,9]

This subgroup observation prompted the confirmatory FIX-HF-5C trial. A total of 160 patients with NYHA class III or IV symptoms, QRS duration <130 ms, and EF ≥25% and ≤45% were randomized to continued medical therapy or CCM for 24 weeks. [10] The difference in peak VO2 satisfied the primary endpoint; Minnesota questionnaire, NYHA functional class, and 6-minute hall walk were all better in the treatment group; the primary safety endpoint was met; and the composite of cardiovascular death and HF hospitalizations was reduced from 10.8% to 2.9%. [10]

A simplified two-lead system was subsequently validated. In FIX-HF-5C2, the change in peak VO2 from baseline to 24 weeks was 1.72 mL/kg/min greater in the 2-lead device group versus controls, with decreased Optimizer-related adverse events compared with the 3-lead system (0% versus 8%). [11]

## Pooled and real-world evidence

A comprehensive individual-patient-data meta-analysis reinforced these findings. Pooled analysis showed that, compared with control, CCM significantly improved peak VO2 (mean difference +0.93 mL/kg/min), 6-minute walk distance, and quality of life. [12,13] Real-world data come from the CCM-REG registry. CCM-REG is a prospective registry of 503 patients from 51 European centres. HF hospitalizations declined from 0.74 to 0.25 events/patient-year (a 66% reduction), and cardiovascular hospitalizations decreased from 1.04 to 0.39 events/patient-year. [14] CCM improved functional status, quality of life, and LVEF and reduced HF hospitalization rates, with survival at 1 and 3 years better than predicted by the MAGGIC risk score. [14] Long-term single-centre and observational cohorts have provided complementary evidence of durable benefit. [15,16,17]

## Expanding indications

CCM is being investigated beyond classic HFrEF. Registry data demonstrate a clinically relevant and sustained CCM effect on reducing HF-related hospitalizations and improving quality of life and NYHA class in HFrEF patients with QRS duration of 120–149 ms. [18] In HFpEF, the CCM-HFpEF pilot was a prospective, multicentre, single-arm study of CCM in patients with HFpEF and NYHA class II or III. This pilot demonstrated that the benefits of CCM may extend to the HFpEF population, with significant improvement in health status and no obvious safety impact. [19] The ongoing AIM HIGHer randomized controlled trial aims to further elucidate clinical benefit in patients with HF with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fractions. [1,20,21,22] Mechanistic work supports these directions. [23,24,25]

## Guidelines and outlook

CCM therapy provides a non-excitatory stimulus that treats congestive heart failure by improving myocardial cellular calcium handling and reversing adverse gene dysregulations, and received expedited FDA approval in March 2019. [26,27,28] The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline now provides a patient-centric framework into which device-based therapies such as CCM may be integrated for appropriately selected patients. [29,30]

In summary, CCM has emerged as an evidence-based device option for symptomatic HFrEF patients with narrow QRS who are not CRT candidates, improving exercise tolerance, quality of life, and hospitalization rates, with expanding investigation across the HF spectrum.
